You are a single test-authoring agent. Your only goal is to write one genuine
pytest regression test for the supplied bug-fix commit. The test must fail at
the broken parent, pass at the fix, exercise behavior changed by the fix, and
avoid collateral changes.

Work empirically. First inspect nearby tests, fixtures, and parent-side source.
Stage a test, run it at the fix, and use the actual failure output to repair it.
Then run it at the parent. If it passes there, tighten the assertion so it
reproduces the reported bug. Use `check_gates` only when the staged test is a
plausible regression test; at most five gate checks are available. A passing
gate check ends the case automatically.

Use only the provided tools. `write_test` can stage one new test file; it cannot
edit repository source or existing tests. Reads and searches always inspect the
broken parent checkout. Read small windows instead of trying to reconstruct
whole files. Prefer existing public APIs and repository fixtures over mocks of
implementation details.

Do not game the transition. In particular, do not inspect source files, git
history, package versions, commit identifiers, environment markers, or the
presence of new symbols at test runtime. Do not use unconditional failures,
intentional import/collection errors, skips, xfails, timing races, or assertions
whose only purpose is to distinguish the two checkouts. The parent failure must
demonstrate the issue's externally observable behavior, and the fix pass must
demonstrate its correction. APIs used by the test must already exist at the
parent unless the issue is explicitly about a newly supported input to an
existing API.

Tool errors are written to help you recover. Follow their suggested next action.
Long tool output ends with an explicit truncation marker; narrow the query or
read another window rather than assuming omitted text is absent.

When you have a credible staged test, call `check_gates`. Do not merely describe
a test in prose. If you cannot produce a credible test within the limits, state
the blocker briefly and stop; never fabricate a passing result.

Case: marshmallow-code/marshmallow#1789
Repository: marshmallow-code/marshmallow
Broken parent: 4041fb47bf0983eb64b3213602b6dd4af0e8da8f
Fixed commit: 721976d2bffa2384db9217bb75569c33f9cadf84

Linked issues:
Issue #1788:
By default `mypy` running in strict mode doesn't allow for untyped functions or decorators to be used. Since all the decorators in `/src/marshmallow/decorators.py` are untyped, the only way to use `mypy` with the `--strict` flag is to add a `# type: ignore` flag on every line referencing any of the decorators. Adding type hints would solve this problem.

Created a pull request here: https://github.com/marshmallow-code/marshmallow/pull/1789

Couldn't really think of any tests since these are just type hint changes. Used `Callable[..., Any]` to be as backwards compatible as possible towards other repos and not use overly convoluted type hints as `post_load` could return something very different from `pre_load`, etc.

The `MarshmallowHook` protocol was based on this `mypy` discussion: https://github.com/python/mypy/issues/2087. The `Protocol` class itself couldn't be used directly due to backwards compatibility issues. Alternatively I can update the PR to avoid the class and use `# type: ignore` on the two lines accessing the `__marshmallow_hook__` property, which normally isn't allowed since a `Callable` doesn't have that property.

Pull request title:
Type hinted all the decorators in marshmallow/decorators.py

Pull request body:
Added a bunch of type hints to the `decorators` module making it easier to use `marshmallow` alongside `mypy` running in strict mode

close #1788

into a parent-side missing-symbol test):

Now I understand the change. The fix adds type annotations to the decorator functions. The key behavioral change is in `set_hook`: at the parent, it directly accesses `fn.__marshmallow_hook__` and sets `fn.__marshmallow_hook__ = hook_config = {}`. At the fix, it uses `cast(MarshmallowHook, fn)` and adds a guard `if hook_config is not None:` before `hook_config[key] = kwargs`.

The `MarshmallowHook` protocol class is introduced with `__marshmallow_hook__` typed as `Optional[Dict[...]]`, and the `cast` allows accessing the attribute. The `if hook_config is not None` guard means that if someone explicitly sets `__marshmallow_hook__ = None` on a function, the fix won't crash trying to write to `None`.

But the real behavioral change is more subtle. Let me think about what could go wrong at the parent that the fix corrects...

Actually, looking more carefully: the parent code does `fn.__marshmallow_hook__ = hook_config = {}` when there's no `__marshmallow_hook__` attribute. The fix does `function.__marshmallow_hook__ = hook_config = {}` (same) but then checks `if hook_config is not None: hook_config[key] = kwargs`.

The key difference: at the parent, if `fn` already has `__marshmallow_hook__` set to `None` (or some non-dict), the `try` succeeds (no AttributeError), `hook_config = None`, and then `hook_config[key] = kwargs` would raise `TypeError: 'NoneType' object does not support item assignment`. The fix guards against this with `if hook_config is not None`.

But more importantly, the type annotations themselves are the main change. Since the issue is about mypy strict mode, the regression test should exercise the runtime behavior that the type annotations enable. However, the instructions say "APIs used by the test must already exist at the parent unless the issue is explicitly about a newly supported input to an existing API."
